outputs.L3:
An organic light-emitting diode comprises two electrodes with different electrical conductivities and an organic layer stack arranged between them. The organic layer stack is configured to generate light when an electrical voltage is applied across the electrodes. In operation, charge carriers are injected from the electrodes into the organic layer stack, where they recombine and emit light, thereby forming a lighting surface.

To support uniform and controlled current flow, the device further includes a highly conductive current distribution layer. This layer assists in distributing electrical current across the device, particularly in areas where one of the electrodes has comparatively lower electrical conductivity. By improving current spreading, the current distribution layer helps influence the brightness distribution over the lighting surface.

In a plan view of the organic light-emitting diode, a plurality of contact regions is arranged outside the outer contour of the organic layer stack. These contact regions are positioned beyond the active light-generating region and serve as defined electrical connection areas. In the contact regions, the second electrode is electrically connected to the current distribution layer, allowing current to be supplied to or distributed through the second electrode via the highly conductive layer.

The device also includes current blocking regions. These regions electrically disconnect the second electrode from the current distribution layer at selected locations. By selectively interrupting electrical contact between the second electrode and the current distribution layer, the current flow into different portions of the second electrode can be controlled. As a result, the luminous intensity across the lighting surface can be adjusted in a targeted manner. This configuration enables a controlled brightness distribution and can be used to improve homogeneity or to create predetermined intensity profiles across the organic light-emitting diode.
outputs.L4:
An organic light-emitting diode (OLED) includes a layer arrangement designed to provide improved control over the distribution of current across the device and, as a result, improved control over the luminous intensity emitted from its lighting surface. The OLED comprises an organic layer stack arranged between a first electrode and a second electrode. The organic layer stack includes at least one organic light-emitting layer which emits light when an electric current flows through the layer stack. The second electrode has a comparatively lower electrical conductivity, while an additional current distribution layer has a comparatively higher electrical conductivity and is provided for distributing current laterally over the device.

The current distribution layer is not connected to the second electrode over the entire surface of the OLED. Instead, electrical contact between the current distribution layer and the second electrode is established only in selected contact regions. These contact regions are arranged outside the contour or outline of the organic layer stack. In the area within the contour of the organic layer stack, current blocking regions are provided between the current distribution layer and the second electrode. These current blocking regions electrically disconnect, or at least substantially electrically isolate, the current distribution layer from the second electrode in those areas.

This arrangement makes it possible to influence where current is injected into or supplied to the second electrode. Since the second electrode has lower conductivity, current introduced at the selected contact regions spreads through the second electrode in a controlled manner before passing through the organic layer stack. The current blocking regions prevent direct electrical connection between the current distribution layer and the second electrode within the active light-emitting area. As a result, uncontrolled or excessive local current injection in the lighting area can be avoided.

By selecting the number, size, shape, and position of the contact regions and the current blocking regions, the current flow through the OLED can be deliberately adjusted. This allows the luminous intensity across the lighting surface to be shaped in a predetermined way. For example, areas that would otherwise appear darker can be supplied with more current, while areas that would otherwise be too bright can be supplied with less current. In this manner, the OLED can be designed to produce a more uniform brightness distribution over a large-area emission surface.

The configuration is particularly useful for large-area OLED lighting devices, in which voltage drops and sheet resistance in the electrodes may otherwise cause visible brightness gradients. The high-conductivity current distribution layer reduces electrical losses and helps distribute current efficiently, while the selective contact regions define controlled current entry points into the lower-conductivity second electrode. The current blocking regions ensure that this distribution is not short-circuited by direct contact across the active area.

Thus, the OLED structure enables both improved brightness uniformity and intentional brightness patterning. Depending on the desired application, the distribution of contact and blocking regions may be optimized to achieve homogeneous illumination, edge compensation, center-brightness correction, or a deliberately non-uniform light output. The result is an OLED device with enhanced optical performance, better current management, and greater flexibility in controlling the emitted light across the lighting surface.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the following invention in patent-style language: an organic light-emitting diode where a low-conductivity electrode contacts a high-conductivity current distribution layer only in selected regions outside the organic stack outline, while other regions are blocked to tune brightness.
counterfactuals.output:
An organic light-emitting diode device comprises an organic electroluminescent stack disposed between first and second electrodes, wherein at least one of the electrodes is a relatively low-conductivity electrode extending across an emission area. A relatively high-conductivity current distribution layer is provided in electrical communication with the low-conductivity electrode only at selected contact regions positioned outside an outline of the organic electroluminescent stack. One or more insulating or blocking regions are interposed between the high-conductivity current distribution layer and the low-conductivity electrode at other locations, thereby preventing electrical contact at such locations.

By selectively defining the contact regions and the blocked regions, lateral current injection into the low-conductivity electrode is spatially controlled. The resulting current distribution across the organic stack, and therefore the luminance profile of the OLED, may be adjusted or tuned. The arrangement permits brightness uniformity correction, intentional brightness shaping, or compensation for resistive voltage drops without requiring direct contact between the high-conductivity layer and the electrode within the active organic emission region.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a technical description of an organic LED structure using reference numerals, including first and second electrodes, an organic light-generating layer stack, a current spreading layer, contact regions, blocking regions, and controlled luminous intensity.
counterfactuals.output:
An organic light-emitting diode (OLED) device 100 comprises a substrate 102, a first electrode 110 disposed over the substrate 102, an organic light-generating layer stack 120 disposed over the first electrode 110, and a second electrode 130 disposed over the organic light-generating layer stack 120. The first electrode 110 and the second electrode 130 are configured to inject charge carriers into the organic light-generating layer stack 120 when a drive voltage is applied between the electrodes 110, 130.

The organic light-generating layer stack 120 may include, in sequence, a hole injection layer 122, a hole transport layer 124, an emissive organic layer 126, an electron transport layer 128, and optionally an electron injection layer 129. The emissive organic layer 126 is configured to generate light in response to recombination of holes and electrons supplied through the first and second electrodes 110, 130. The light generated by the emissive organic layer 126 may be emitted through the substrate 102, through the second electrode 130, or through both sides of the OLED device 100, depending on whether the electrodes 110, 130 are transparent, semi-transparent, or reflective.

A current spreading layer 140 is electrically coupled to the first electrode 110 and extends laterally over at least a portion of the OLED device 100. The current spreading layer 140 is configured to reduce lateral voltage drop across the first electrode 110 and to improve uniform distribution of current supplied to the organic light-generating layer stack 120. In one implementation, the current spreading layer 140 comprises a conductive transparent oxide, a thin metal layer, a metal grid, a conductive polymer, graphene, or a combination thereof. The current spreading layer 140 may have a sheet resistance lower than that of the first electrode 110, thereby promoting lateral current spreading.

The OLED device 100 further includes a plurality of contact regions 150 and a plurality of blocking regions 160 arranged between the current spreading layer 140 and the first electrode 110. Each contact region 150 provides an electrical connection between the current spreading layer 140 and the first electrode 110. Each blocking region 160 electrically separates the current spreading layer 140 from the first electrode 110 in a corresponding area, thereby locally inhibiting direct current injection from the current spreading layer 140 into the first electrode 110.

The contact regions 150 and blocking regions 160 may be patterned to define a predetermined lateral current distribution within the first electrode 110. For example, the contact regions 150 may have different sizes, spacings, or densities across the OLED device 100. Regions requiring higher luminous output may include a higher density of contact regions 150, while regions requiring lower luminous output may include a lower density of contact regions 150 or larger blocking regions 160. In this manner, the local current density delivered to the organic light-generating layer stack 120 is controlled by the pattern of electrical coupling between the current spreading layer 140 and the first electrode 110.

The blocking regions 160 may comprise an electrically insulating material, such as silicon oxide, silicon nitride, aluminum oxide, an organic dielectric, a photoresist material, or another non-conductive layer. Alternatively, the blocking regions 160 may be formed by locally removing, oxidizing, or otherwise modifying the current spreading layer 140 or an interface layer so as to prevent electrical contact in selected regions. The contact regions 150 may be formed by openings in the blocking regions 160, by conductive vias, by direct overlap between the current spreading layer 140 and the first electrode 110, or by locally deposited conductive interconnect material.

During operation, a driving circuit 170 applies an electrical potential between the first electrode 110 and the second electrode 130. Current supplied through the current spreading layer 140 enters the first electrode 110 primarily through the contact regions 150 and is laterally distributed through the first electrode 110 before passing through the organic light-generating layer stack 120 to the second electrode 130. The amount of current injected into each local portion of the organic light-generating layer stack 120 determines the corresponding local luminous intensity. Accordingly, by selecting the geometry and spatial distribution of the contact regions 150 and the blocking regions 160, the OLED device 100 provides controlled luminous intensity over its emitting surface.

In one embodiment, the contact regions 150 are arranged with a first pitch P1 in a central region 180 of the OLED device 100 and with a second pitch P2 in a peripheral region 182 of the OLED device 100. The first pitch P1 may differ from the second pitch P2 to compensate for edge effects, electrode resistance, optical nonuniformity, or desired luminance gradients. In another embodiment, the contact regions 150 have varying contact areas A1, A2, A3 to provide graded electrical coupling between the current spreading layer 140 and the first electrode 110. The resulting graded current injection produces a corresponding controlled spatial distribution of luminous intensity.

The OLED structure 100 may therefore be configured to provide uniform luminance, deliberately nonuniform luminance, edge compensation, pixel-free brightness shaping, or decorative illumination patterns without requiring separate individually driven pixels. The controlled luminous intensity is achieved structurally by the patterned arrangement of the contact regions 150 and blocking regions 160 in combination with the current spreading layer 140 and the first electrode 110.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
